_about: Single source of truth for every rendering, and the auditable term ledger (check 5). ONE rendering per referent for the whole book. Before you romanize any name, check here AND authority.json (the cross-book ledger). status per entry: 'attested' (form used in English scholarship, give the citation in note), 'provisional' (your romanization, not found in outside sources), 'decided' (a project style call). Keys starting with '_' are ignored. Seeded at the survey from authority.json; enriched per batch. Bylines/contributors are added as each article is translated.

杜月笙.cast: 1888–1951; the foremost of Shanghai's ‘three big bosses,’ a Green Gang chief who rose from a fruit-stall boy to a power broker between the underworld, the concessions and the Nationalist state. The subject of seven articles here.
杜月笙.note: 1888–1951. Foremost of the Shanghai Green Gang ‘three tycoons.’ Pinyin form standard across the collection.

黄金荣.cast: 1868–1953; the senior of the three bosses, and the only Chinese chief detective of the French Concession police. Three articles here.
黄金荣.note: Green Gang boss and the sole Chinese chief inspector of the French Concession detective squad; Chiang Kai-shek was once nominally his disciple.

张啸林.cast: 1877–1940; the third of the three bosses, a Hangzhou-born strongman; later a collaborator with the Japanese, assassinated in 1940.
张啸林.note: One of the ‘three big bosses’ of the Shanghai gangs, with Huang Jinrong and Du Yuesheng.

顾竹轩.cast: b. 1885; Green Gang boss of the Zhabei district, rickshaw-fleet magnate and owner of the Tianchan Stage; sheltered Communist underground workers.
顾竹轩.note: Jiangsu-born gang figure who dominated Zhabei; two articles here treat his rise and his cover for revolutionary work.

张仁奎.cast: 1865–1944; a senior Green Gang master of the ‘Big’ (Da) generation whose disciples filled Shanghai; founder of the Ren Society.
张仁奎.note: Elder Green Gang figure; Du Yuesheng and many others were ranked below his generation.

戴笠.cast: 1897–1946; head of the Nationalists' secret service (the Juntong); Du Yuesheng's wartime partner.
戴笠.note: Head of the Nationalists' Bureau of Investigation and Statistics (军统/Juntong), the KMT secret police.

朱学范.note: 1905–1996; postal-workers’ leader who rose through the Green Gang and the Nationalist labour apparatus, broke with the Kuomintang in 1948, and became a minister and vice-chairman of the NPC Standing Committee in the People’s Republic. Author of this article and calligrapher of the book’s title.

陆京士.note: d. 1975; Du Yuesheng’s foremost disciple in the labour world, boss of the postal union and a Nationalist party and Garrison Command official; the author’s colleague and rival. Followed the Kuomintang to Taiwan.

李立三.note: 1899–1967; early Communist labour organizer, a leader of the May Thirtieth Movement and briefly the Party’s top leader (the ‘Li Lisan line,’ 1930).

杨度.note: 1875–1931; classical scholar who championed constitutional monarchy under Yuan Shikai, then reinvented himself—joining the Communist Party in secret in 1929 while serving as an adviser to Du Yuesheng. His CCP membership was made public only in 1975.

李大钊.note: 1889–1927; co-founder of the Chinese Communist Party. Seized from the Soviet embassy in Beijing and hanged on Zhang Zuolin’s orders in April 1927.

赵朴初.note: 1907–2000; Buddhist lay leader, poet, and relief organizer; secretly aided the Communist underground through Shanghai’s charitable and refugee bodies in the war years, and later headed the Buddhist Association of China.

闻兰亭.note: Green Gang figure prominent in Shanghai commercial and charitable circles; used by the underground through the wartime relief committees, later pressed into a puppet commercial-control post.

向海潜.note: 1888–1974; also called Xiang Songpo; a leader of the Hongmen (the ‘Five Lakes’ lodges) and a veteran of the 1911 Revolution.

张克昌.note: Postal-union gangster and the author’s fellow disciple under Du Yuesheng; founder of the Chang Society (畅社), who went over to the puppet Wang Jingwei regime as a deputy minister.

金廷荪.note: Green Gang figure and Du Yuesheng associate; patron of the Ming Society (铭社), one of the disciple-societies modelled on Du’s Heng Society.

章士钊.note: 1881–1973; scholar, lawyer, and sometime Beiyang education minister who named Du Yuesheng’s Heng Society; later a noted public figure in the People’s Republic.

汪精卫.note: 1883–1944; senior Nationalist leader who in 1938 defected to Japan and headed the collaborationist ‘reorganized’ government at Nanjing; his name is a byword in these pages for the puppet regime.

吴成方.note: Author of this article; a Communist underground organizer who ran united-front work with gang and secret-society figures in Beijing and Shanghai from the 1920s to the 1940s.

胡鄂公.note: 1884–1951; also known as Hu Nanhu; a 1911 revolutionary and Beiyang official who joined the Communist Party in the 1920s and worked the united front among old revolutionaries and gang figures.

翁文灏.note: 1889–1971; geologist and Nationalist official, acting president of Tsinghua University in 1931 and later premier; returned to the mainland in 1951.

冯玉祥.note: 1882–1948; the ‘Christian general,’ a warlord who at times allied with the Nationalists, the Soviets, and the left; organized the short-lived Chahar People’s Anti-Japanese Allied Army in 1933.

李世瑜.note: 1922–2010; folklorist and historian of Chinese popular religion and secret societies, author of this study of the Green Gang.

姜豪.note: The author of the second study; a Baoshan-born Kuomintang figure and initiated Green Gang member of the ‘Da’ generation who writes here partly from the inside.

金幼孜.note: The gang legend’s ‘first patriarch.’ A real Ming official (1368–1431), Grand Secretary under the Yongle emperor; the gang genealogy built around him is legend.

罗清.note: The gang legend’s ‘second patriarch,’ conflated with Patriarch Luo, founder of the Luo (Non-Action) sect.

潘清.note: Of the three founder-patriarchs, Pan is reckoned the chief; Green Gang men called one another ‘the Pan brothers.’

王伦.note: d. 1774; leader of the Clear Water sect (a White Lotus offshoot) whose 1774 rising at Linqing drew on the grain-transport boatmen.

杨虎.note: Also named Xiaotian; Songhu garrison commander and Green Gang figure.

向松坡.note: Xiang Haiqian; see the note at his first appearance.

薛耕莘.note: The author of this chapter; the byline prints the variant graph 畊 for 耕.

川岛芳子.note: See the note at her first appearance.

袁寒云.cast: 1889–1931; the poet, collector and Green Gang celebrity Yuan Kewen, second son of Yuan Shikai, who opposed his father's monarchy. The subject of ch10, told by his disciple Chen Timin.
袁寒云.note: Yuan Kewen (袁克文), hao Hanyun; pinyin form used across the collection.

程锡文.note: Narrator of ch13; Huang Jinrong’s household steward, who tells the family from the inside.

杨展成.note: Recorder who set down Cheng Xiwen’s ch13 account.

黄振世.note: Narrator of ch14; a fishery-company manager, Huang disciple and later a standing director of the Rong Society, who writes as a self-confessed insider.

何国涛.note: Recorder who set down Huang Zhenshi’s ch14 account.

林桂生.note: Huang Jinrong’s first wife as named in ch13; a formidable figure in her own right. ch14 and later scholarship give her surname as Lin; the source’s own editors flag the variant Ye Guisheng. See the note at ch14.

叶桂生.note: Huang Jinrong’s first wife as named by the ch14 narrator; the source’s editors add that one account gives her as Lin Guisheng (so ch13). Rendered as each narrator prints; the discrepancy is footnoted.

范开泰.note: “Ebony Kaitai,” a City God Temple man about town and temple director; his wife was Shi Jinxiu.

史锦绣.note: “Bandit Jinxiu,” a formidable Changzhou woman of the City God Temple demi-monde, sworn sister to Huang’s first wife.

范回春.note: Younger brother of Fan Kaitai; a bank manager and deputy manager of the Sanxin opium combine.

徐福生.note: “Havoc-in-Heaven Fusheng,” a Suzhou-Creek wharf hoodlum and Huang disciple, said to have introduced Huang Jinrong to Sun Yat-sen.

张方庚.note: A Huang disciple who ran the Dacheng leather-goods company.

韩荣浦.note: A Wu Peifu adjutant whose stray tip, in Huang’s telling, cracked the Bishop Yao kidnapping; later a go-between to Yuan Kewen.

马雨亭.note: A Huang disciple skilled at making rigged gambling gear.

徐阿东.note: The French police hoodlum-squad foreman whom Huang and Du brought to heel, a turning point in the men-about-town’s rise.

陈培德.note: Huang Jinrong’s favored disciple, a British-American Tobacco union chairman; his arrest by Du Yuesheng’s man Lu Jingshi sharpened the Huang–Du feud.

陈福康.note: Manager of the Huang household’s real estate and the Great World accounts; head of a rival clique to the narrator within Huang’s gate.

邱子嘉.note: Works manager of the Renfeng mill and a core Zhongxin/Rong Society organizer allied with the narrator.

王兴高.note: The Subei disciple of Gu Zhuxuan who shot Tang Jiapeng dead at the Great World gate.

周信芳.note: 1895–1975; the great Peking-opera actor known by his stage name Qilintong (麒麟童), who took Huang Jinrong as master for protection against Gu Zhuxuan.

常春恒.note: A wenwu-laosheng Peking-opera actor beaten to death on Gu Zhuxuan’s order in a salary dispute at the Tianchan Stage.

吴世宝.note: “Killer Taibao,” guard chief of the Japanese puppet secret service at No. 76 Jessfield Road; his open threats cowed even the concession detective-chiefs.

余爱珍.note: Wife of Wu Shibao; the shooting of her bodyguard by a Settlement constable in May 1941 was a notorious “76” incident.

潘七分.note: Styled Zixin (子欣); a Tianjin gang chief in Huang’s wide network. Huang trusted him in his last years and called him “Old Seventh Pan.” The ch14 narrator prints his name both as Pan Qifen and, at his first mention, Pan Zixin.

潘子欣.note: See Pan Qifen; the Tianjin gang chief is named both ways in ch14, rendered as printed.

杭州阿法.note: A grand hoodlum of the early Republic raised up by Huang Jinrong, who monopolized opium delivery on the Shiliupu wharves; the source notes a variant graph 阿发.

马鸿魁.note: The “Night-soil King” of the French Concession, a Huang disciple. Not the Ningxia warlord Ma Hongkui (马鸿逵).

唐嘉鹏.note: Manager of the Great World and one of the two great pillars of Huang’s gate; murdered in the feud with Gu Zhuxuan’s faction.

丁永昌.note: A trusted Huang disciple who ran the Great World and carried out kidnappings for him.

鲁锦臣.note: A close Huang disciple and French-police detective-chief who attended the old man in his retirement.

庞京周.note: A prominent Shanghai physician, Du Yuesheng's personal doctor.

李祖夔.note: A former magistrate of Shanghai county.

陈布雷.note: 1890–1948; Chiang Kai-shek's confidential secretary and chief speechwriter.

吴稚晖.note: 1865–1953; veteran Kuomintang elder and calligrapher; also written 吴敬恒.

吴敬恒.note: The formal given name of the Kuomintang elder better known by his courtesy name, Wu Zhihui; the same man.

唐绍仪.note: 1862–1938; first premier of the Republic; assassinated in Shanghai after contacts with the Japanese.

高宗武.note: A Nationalist diplomat active in the secret peace talks with Japan that led to Wang Jingwei's defection.

杨杰.note: 1889–1949; Nationalist general who turned against Chiang; assassinated by Juntong agents on the eve of the Communist victory.

吴开先.note: A leading member of the CC Clique in Shanghai.

胡宗南.note: 1896–1962; the Nationalist general who commanded the northwest.

朱子桥.note: General Zhu Qinglan, a noted relief philanthropist of the Republican era.

张嘉璈.note: Chang Kia-ngau (1889–1979), the banker and financial administrator.

梅乐斯.note: 1900–1961; U.S. Navy officer, head of the American side of the Sino-American Cooperation Organization.

王新衡.note: A Juntong department head and Du Yuesheng's channel to Dai Li.

吴绍澍.note: Du's disciple turned rival; postwar vice-mayor of Shanghai who publicly broke with him.

毛人凤.note: Dai Li's successor as head of the Baomiju secret service.

蒋经国.note: 1910–1988; Chiang Kai-shek's elder son, later president of the Republic of China on Taiwan; here the enforcer of the 1948 gold-yuan reform in Shanghai.

孔令侃.note: H. H. Kung's son and chairman of the Yangtze Company; Chiang Ching-kuo's cousin.

宋美龄.note: 1898–2003; Madame Chiang Kai-shek, sister of T. V. Soong and aunt of Kong Lingkan.

方治.note: A CC Clique figure; chairman of the Shanghai municipal party headquarters.

俞飞鹏.note: A Chiang confidant who headed wartime transport.

黄国栋.note: Chief accountant of the Du Yuesheng household and the narrator of this article; son of Huang Wenxiang.

罗醴泉.note: Took down Huang Guodong's oral account.

黄文祥.note: The narrator's father; the Du household accountant before him.

杨渔笙.note: The Du household accountant before Huang Wenxiang; fled during the war and broke with Du.

陈帼英.note: Du Yuesheng's second wife (‘the Fifth’), a Suzhou woman.

孙佩豪.note: Du Yuesheng's third wife (‘the Seventh’), a Suzhou woman.

万墨林.note: Du Yuesheng's household steward and chief factotum; ran Du's Shanghai affairs during the war and was seized by the puppet secret service.

万兆棠.note: Elder brother of Wan Molin, styled Duxin; the household post passed from him to his brother.

翁佐卿.note: A Du household secretary, disciple of Zhang Xiaolin.

邱访陌.note: A Du household secretary, introduced by Chen Qun; later a puppet income-tax official.

陆桂才.note: A Du bodyguard, disciple of Zhang Xiaolin, known as Lu the Pockmarked.

陈秦鹤.note: A Du bodyguard, a Taizhou man-about-town.

郁访熏.note: The man who prepared Du Yuesheng's opium pipes, styled Yongfu.

黄炎培.note: 1878–1965. Educator and founder of the China Democratic National Construction Association; a frequent guest of Du's who did wartime liaison work.

高士奎.note: A Hongmen elder kept at Du's expense.

朱文德.note: One of the four Du men left to run Shanghai affairs during the war.

王晓籁.note: A leading figure of the Shanghai General Chamber of Commerce.

潘公展.note: Nationalist CC Clique figure and newspaperman in Shanghai.

唐世昌.note: A Du disciple; manager of the Shen Bao and Xinwen Bao, through whom Du influenced the Shanghai press.

章荣初.note: A Du disciple; manager of the Qingfeng Cotton Mill.

邵子英.note: A Du disciple; interpreter for the French utilities, who organized the 1932 strike weapon for Du.

谢葆生.note: A Green Gang secondary figure; ballroom and theater proprietor.

杨顺铨.note: The Shiliupu ‘fish tyrant,’ nicknamed Fish-monger Little Shun.

江肇铭.note: A Du disciple nicknamed ‘the Xuantong Emperor,’ who ran a gambling house on Avenue Foch.

卢小嘉.note: Son of the Zhejiang military governor Lu Yongxiang; his quarrel with Huang Jinrong over the actress Lu Lanchun led to Huang's arrest and Du's rescue of him.

朱葆三.note: A prominent Ningbo-Shanghai comprador and financier.

李应生.note: A Chinese member of the French Concession Municipal Council.

蒋伯诚.note: A Nationalist figure who kept liaison with Du's Shanghai men during the war.

汪曼云.note: A Shanghai figure who later collaborated with the Wang Jingwei regime.

王民休.note: A democratic-party liaison man in wartime Shanghai, using the alias Li Dacheng.

傅品圭.note: A Zhonghui Bank manager; son of the puppet mayor Fu Xiao'an.

傅筱庵.note: 1872–1940. Mayor of the Japanese puppet Shanghai municipal government; assassinated in 1940.

徐庆云.note: Father of Xu Maotang, the Zhonghui Bank manager.

唐生智.note: 1889–1970. Nationalist general, commander of the defense of Nanjing in 1937.

林康侯.note: One of the ‘three notables of Shanghai’ during the occupation.

蔡庆其.note: A Taiwanese who bailed the narrator out and drew him into the occupation-era social round.

马连良.note: 1901–1966. Celebrated Peking-opera actor of the old-man (laosheng) roles.

黄振东.note: A Du disciple and lavish gift-giver.

周祥生.note: Founder of the Johnson (Xiangsheng) Taxi Company in Shanghai.

周恩霆.note: A disciple Du took on in Chongqing; said to have been a cousin of Zhou Enlai.

宋霭龄.note: Eldest of the Soong sisters, wife of H. H. Kung and mother of Kong Lingkan.

盛丕华.note: 1882–1961. Shanghai industrialist and democratic figure; after 1949 a deputy mayor of Shanghai.

潘汉年.note: 1906–1977. Chinese Communist intelligence chief; after 1949 a deputy mayor of Shanghai, purged in 1955.

张澜.note: 1872–1955. Chairman of the China Democratic League; in 1949 a vice-chairman of the Central People's Government.

史良.note: 1900–1985. Woman jurist, one of the ‘seven gentlemen’ arrested in 1936; later the PRC's first minister of justice.

简照南.note: Founder of the Nanyang Brothers Tobacco Company.

廖承志.note: 1908–1983. Chinese Communist leader active in overseas and united-front work.

郁咏馥.note: The narrator of this chapter: Du Yuesheng's opium-pipe attendant for some twenty years. Romanization provisional; name crop-verified from the byline and the source footnote (both 郁咏馥, not the OCR 郁咏敌/郁咏禾).

汤玉麟.note: 1871–1949; warlord governor of Rehe (Jehol), notorious for the opium trade. Attested form.

史量才.note: 1880–1934; owner of the Shenbao, assassinated 1934 on Chiang Kai-shek's orders.

张学良.note: 1901–2001; the ‘Young Marshal.’ Courtesy name Hanqing (汉卿).

田洪元.note: Accountant at the Commercial Bank who kept Du supplied with bank drafts; provisional romanization.

顾鳌.note: 1879–1949; a Beiyang-era politician styled a ‘meritorious servant of the Hongxian’ monarchy; here one of Du's opium-smoking retainers, called ‘Secretary Gu.’

唐缴之.note: Named in ch17 alongside Luo Qinghua as one of Du's business-world ‘feelers.’ The middle character (缴) reads uncertainly in the scan; romanization provisional.

毛子坚.note: A Nanshi gangster-gentleman who borrowed the City God's sedan-chairs for the Du temple procession; provisional.

焦文彬.note: The Du household accountant before Huang Guodong; provisional.

黄国法.note: Younger son of Huang Wenxiang, placed by Du in the Zhonghui Bank; brother of the ch16 narrator Huang Guodong.

小兰英.note: Yao Yulan's foster-mother, a noted actress in old-male (laosheng) roles; provisional.

玉英.note: Yao Yulan's foster-sister, whom Du first meant to take; she died young. Provisional.

王彬彦.note: A Subei performer who invited Du to a charity benefit; provisional.

杜镛.note: Du Yuesheng's formal given name (镛); the two characters he practiced signing after becoming a company chairman.

杜维仁.note: A son named in ch17 as remaining in Shanghai after liberation; not in ch16's fuller enumeration of Du's sons (see note). Provisional.

杭州阿发.note: A hoodlum companion of young Du around Shiliupu; a by-name, provisional.

黄永言.note: The narrator of this chapter; provisional romanization.

杨在田.note: A salt-trader nicknamed ‘Sea-Churning Golden Dragon,’ founder of the Yongji/Datong shipping line; gang-senior to Du.

张慰慈.note: Zhang Cha's grandson, acting manager of Dada; provisional.

鲍心斋.note: The old-school manager of Dada, forced out after the Deji bank failure; provisional.

蒋敬堂.note: A Dada standing director who briefly acted as chairman; provisional.

沈燕谋.note: A Zhang-family relative, general manager of the Dasheng mills and briefly of Dada; provisional.

沈敬夫.note: Shen Yanmou's grandfather, in-law of Zhang Cha; provisional.

徐陶菴.note: Yang Guanbei's uncle by marriage, a Dada director and manager of the Nantong Flour Mill; provisional.

徐揭和.note: Xu Tao'an's son, US-educated, made a Dada director; provisional.

沈华亭.note: A steamship-company comprador who took a gang ‘old man’; provisional.

黄慕宗.note: A China Merchants captain who became a gang ‘mountain lord’; provisional.

俞仙亭.note: Chair of the China Merchants Five-Wharf staff union, a pupil of Du's; provisional.

李公朴.note: 1902–1946; educator and democracy activist, assassinated by Nationalist agents in 1946; here head of a Northern Expedition army liaison section.

吴醒亚.note: A CC-clique Nationalist official; head of the Shanghai Bureau of Social Affairs in the 1930s.

蔡劲军.note: 1900–1985; Shanghai's chief of police / garrison figure in the mid-1930s.

许沅.note: A former Shanghai commissioner of foreign affairs, brought in to mediate the wharf dispute; provisional.

郑锡棠.note: Comprador of the British Gongmao firm and proprietor of the Ping'an Steamship Company; provisional.

李耀庭.note: Deputy manager of Ping'an and manager of the Yixiang Bureau, bought over by Yang Guanbei; provisional.

杨庆邦.note: Dada's customs-clearance man, promoted to keep him loyal; provisional.

寰仲符.note: A nominee in whose name the Datong ship was registered; provisional.

陆伯鸿.note: 1875–1937; the Catholic industrialist and philanthropist, a papal knight; co-founder of the Datong line.

朱志尧.note: 1863–1955; the Catholic industrialist (Kiangnan Dock, machine works), co-founder of the Datong line.

徐忠信.note: Proprietor of the Daxing Steamship Company, a Ningbo associate of Yu Qiaqing; provisional.

吴颙.note: Chief of the Shanghai Shipping Administration; provisional.

黄静泉.note: Huang Zhendong's father, a Java-sugar merchant; provisional.

毕芳来.note: A Guangdong Road provisions dealer paraded for selling Japanese goods; provisional.

宣纯叔.note: One of Du's men installed at Dada; provisional.

阎瑞邬.note: One of Du's men installed at Dada; provisional.

陈润青.note: One of Du's men installed at Dada; provisional.

尹志衡.note: A Boycott Association man shot as a scapegoat; provisional.

叶鸿英.note: 1860–1937; a Shanghai merchant and philanthropist, target of a boycott-era squeeze.

郭兰馨.note: 郭兰馨; the author of this article, a Heng Society member who served as chief secretary at the Hong Kong head office of the Chinese Red Cross under Du. Spelling of the given name provisional (OCR/scan).

邱方柏.note: 邱方柏; one of Du's secretaries, a Fujianese whose real name a source footnote gives as Qiu Fangmo (邱访陌). Provisional.

黄涵之.note: 黄涵之 (1875–1961); Shanghai Buddhist layman and philanthropist, an associate of Guan Jiongzhi.

赵君豪.note: 赵君豪; Shanghai journalist and editor of the Republican period.

张石川.note: 张石川 (1890–1953); pioneering Chinese film director and a founder of the Mingxing Film Company.

杨庆山.note: 杨庆山; a leading gang boss of Hankou.

徐子为.note: 徐子为; a Wujiang man who had assisted Huang Yanpei with documents; made a Tongji Company branch manager. Provisional.

林仁磨.note: 林仁磨; son-in-law of Xu Caicheng. Given name uncertain (scan).

钱大钧.note: 钱大钧 (1893–1982); Kuomintang general, at this time mayor of Shanghai.

鄂森.note: 鄂森; a Shanghai lawyer active in the Pudong Native-Place Association.

徐大统.note: 徐大统; a Heng Society member who made a fortune in paper during the war, nicknamed the ‘Paper King.’

陶雪生.note: 陶雪生; a wartime collaborator (hanjian) whose sealed property the Heng Society bought.

程砚秋.note: 程砚秋 (1904–1958); one of the ‘Four Great Dan’ of Peking opera, founder of the Cheng school of dan roles.

赵荣琛.note: 赵荣琛 (1916–1996); leading exponent of the Cheng school of Peking-opera dan roles.

杨畹侬.note: 杨畹侬; a noted Peking-opera amateur (piaoyou) of the Mei school. Reading of the given name provisional.

金素雯.note: 金素雯 (1917–1990); Peking-opera and stage actress.

谷正纲.note: 谷正纲 (1902–1993); Kuomintang politician, later long the head of anti-Communist relief work on Taiwan.

王懋功.note: 王懋功 (1891–1961); Kuomintang general, at this time chairman of Jiangsu Province.

陶希圣.note: 陶希圣 (1899–1988); historian and politician who, with Gao Zongwu, broke with Wang Jingwei and exposed the secret Sino-Japanese peace terms in the 1940 ‘Gao–Tao Incident.’ The article calls both men traitors for their earlier role in the Wang camp.

张一麐.note: 张一麐 (1867–1943); Suzhou elder statesman, once a secretary to Yuan Shikai, later a patriotic notable.

陈铭枢.note: 陈铭枢 (1889–1965); Kuomintang general, a leader of the 1933 Fujian Rebellion.

杨云史.note: 杨云史 (1875–1941); poet, who served as a secretary to the warlord Wu Peifu.

吴佩孚.note: 吴佩孚 (1874–1939); major warlord of the Zhili clique in the 1920s.

钱永铭.note: 钱永铭, styled Xinzhi; the banker known throughout as Qian Xinzhi, general manager of the Bank of Communications.

徐亮.note: 徐亮, also known as Xu Weibin; a Juntong figure.

青帮.note: 青帮; the great secret-society brotherhood of the lower Yangtze and Shanghai. Rendered ‘Green Gang’ across the collection.

洪门.note: 洪门; the sworn-brotherhood secret society of south China (the ‘Red Gang,’ 洪帮). Kept as Hongmen across the collection.

恒社.note: 恒社; Du Yuesheng's mutual-aid society, founded 1932, through which he organized his following. Its charter and 1934 member roll are the book's appendices.

仁社.note: 仁社; the society founded around the elder gang master Zhang Renkui, a counterpart to Du Yuesheng's Heng Society.

军统.note: 军统; the Nationalists' Bureau of Investigation and Statistics (secret service). Cross-shelf rendering is unsettled (Military Statistics Bureau / the Juntong); this book's rendering is decided at the batch that translates ch21 and reconciled into authority.json then.

毅社.note: 毅社; the disciple-society the author founded in 1934–36 among Shanghai unionists, modelled on Du Yuesheng’s Heng Society; its emblem punned on the author’s name, Zhu Xuefan.

畅社.note: 畅社; the rival postal disciple-society founded by Zhang Kechang.

别动队.note: 别动队; the irregular units raised from Green Gang and Hongmen men during the 1937 Battle of Shanghai, armed and run in connection with Dai Li’s secret service.

天地会.note: The Tiandihui, the great anti-Qing sworn-brotherhood movement of south China, aiming to ‘overthrow the Qing and restore the Ming’; part of the Hongmen tradition.

安庆道友会.note: The Anqing Daoyou Hui, rendered ‘the Anqing Fellowship of the Way’; the fuller early form of the Green Gang, from which the names An-Qing Gang, Clear Gang, and Green Gang evolved.

荣社.note: Huang Jinrong’s disciple-organization, its name taken from his.

忠义救国军.note: A Dai Li / Juntong-affiliated irregular force active in the lower Yangtze during the war.

致公堂.note: The overseas Hongmen lodge network; Cantonese romanization.

忠信社.note: “Loyalty and Faith” Society; the disciple-society Huang Jinrong let his men form in 1936 to undermine Du Yuesheng’s Heng Society. Named from the “learning, conduct, loyalty, faith” tablet in Chiang Kai-shek’s hand at the Huang garden; revived after the war as the Rong Society.

益社.note: The disciple-fraternity Fan Shaozeng, this chapter's narrator, ran in Shanghai on the model of Du Yuesheng's Heng Society.

港济公司.note: The opium-trafficking front company Du set up with Dai Li in 1939, with offices in Chongqing and Hong Kong, nominally under Gu Jiatang.

通济公司.note: The wartime trading company (c. 1943) fronted by Du for Dai Li, smuggling goods to and from the occupied areas under cover of Juntong privilege.

扬子公司.note: Kong Lingkan's Shanghai firm, a byword for wartime and postwar profiteering under the protection of H. H. Kung.

保密局.note: The Bureau of Confidential Affairs, the 1946 renaming of the Juntong secret service.

洪帮.note: The other great Chinese secret-society tradition beside the Green Gang; weaker in Shanghai, stronger in the north.

中汇银行.note: Du Yuesheng's own bank (the China & Overseas Bank), a pillar of his finances. Rendered ‘Zhonghui Bank’ across the collection.

正始中学.note: A school Du Yuesheng ran and subsidized; Chen Qun was its principal.

大东书局.note: A major Shanghai publishing house; Du Weiping was its deputy general manager.

祥生汽车公司.note: A leading Shanghai taxi firm (Johnson Taxi), founded by Zhou Xiangsheng.

南洋兄弟烟草公司.note: One of China's largest cigarette makers, founded by the Jian brothers.

招商局.note: The China Merchants Steam Navigation Company.

通商银行.note: The Commercial Bank of China (中国通商银行), of whose board Du became chairman.

大运公司.note: The company set up to run the aviation-lottery monopoly, with Jin Tingsun as GM.

江苏长途汽车公司.note: A firm Wang Xiaolai managed by Du's arrangement.

大达轮船公司.note: Zhang Jian's Nantong shipping line, the company Du broke into.

大通仁记航业公司.note: Yang Zaitian's Subei-route rival, later Dada's ally.

益祥轮船局.note: A shell bureau used to register the ex-Datong ship.

永济航业公司.note: Yang Zaitian's original salt-trade shipping firm.

大生纱厂.note: Zhang Jian's cotton mills at Nantong, a landmark of early Chinese industry.

怡和洋行.note: The British trading house Jardine, Matheson and Co. (Chinese hong-name Ewo). Book form "Jardine Matheson", per ch07/ch18; ch03 uses the colloquial "Jardine’s" in a factory list.

渣华公司.note: The Dutch Java-China-Japan Line (JCJL / Koninklijke Java-China-Paketvaart Lijnen).

汉冶萍煤铁公司.en: the Hanyeping Coal and Iron Company

山下株式会社.note: The Japanese shipping firm Yamashita Kisen K.K.

江南造船厂.note: The Jiangnan (Kiangnan) Dock and shipyard in Shanghai.

大中华旅馆.note: A Shanghai hotel of which Dai Buxiang was proprietor.

得记钱庄.note: The Nantong native bank whose failure cost Dada its deposit; provisional.

滋丰钱庄.note: The Shanghai native bank through which Dada shares were bought for Du; provisional.

交通银行.note: One of China's major government banks.

上海市社会局.en: the Shanghai Municipal Bureau of Social Affairs
上海市社会局.note: The city bureau Du used to force Dada's reorganization.

交通部.note: The Nationalist ministry over railways, posts and shipping.

上海航业公会.note: The shipowners' guild, treated by Yu Qiaqing as his instrument.

经济绝交大同盟.en: the Grand Alliance for Economic Severance
经济绝交大同盟.note: The anti-Japanese boycott body, nicknamed the ‘Boycott Association.’

南通面粉厂.note: A Zhang-family mill managed by Xu Tao'an.

祥茂洋行.note: A British trading firm whose shipping was crushed by Dada; provisional.

公茂洋行.note: A British firm; Zheng Xitang was its comprador; provisional.

兴中学会.note: 兴中学会; Yang Hu's disciple society.

铭社.note: 铭社; Jin Tingsun's disciple society.

升社.note: 升社; Wang Xiaolai's disciple society.

侠义社.note: 侠义社; Zheng Ziliang's disciple society.

苏浙行动委员会.note: 苏浙行动委员会; its Special Action Corps (别动队) was a Dai Li–organized irregular force raised in the 1937 Shanghai fighting.

中国新社会事业建设协会.en: the China New Social Enterprise Construction Association
中国新社会事业建设协会.pinyin: Zhongguo Xin Shehui Shiye Jianshe Xiehui

花纱布公司.en: the Cotton, Yarn and Cloth Company
花纱布公司.note: 花纱布公司; the government Cotton, Yarn and Cloth Company, which controlled textile supply in the wartime rear.

亲社.note: 亲社; a sub-society of workers formed by Zhu Xuefan.

靖社.note: 靖社; a sub-society formed by Bian Dingyuan.

伦社.note: 伦社; Xu Datong's private club, donated to the Heng Society after the war.

申报馆.note: 申报馆; the office of the Shen Bao (Shun Pao), Shanghai's leading daily newspaper.

三青团.en: the Three People's Principles Youth Corps

纳税华人会.note: 纳税华人会; the Chinese Ratepayers' Association of the French Concession, which elected Chinese members to the French Municipal Council.

法公董局.note: 法公董局; the Conseil d'administration municipale, governing body of the French Concession; its Chinese members were called 华董.

正言报.note: 正言报; a Shanghai newspaper run by Wu Shaoshu in the postwar takeover period.

花纱布管制局.en: the Cotton, Yarn and Cloth Control Bureau
花纱布管制局.pinyin: the Cotton, Yarn and Cloth Control Bureau

国防部保密局.en: the Ministry of National Defense's Bureau of Confidential Investigation
国防部保密局.pinyin: the Ministry of National Defense's Bureau of Confidential Investigation

十六铺.note: The wharf-and-market quarter on the Huangpu at the edge of the old Chinese city, Shanghai's busiest goods landing; where Du Yuesheng got his start.

华格臬路.note: A street in the French Concession, today's Ninghai West Road; site of Du Yuesheng's chief residence.

杜美路.note: A French Concession street, today's Donghu Road.

哈同花园.note: Aili Garden, the vast Nanjing Road estate of the Baghdadi-Jewish tycoon Silas Hardoon.

福煦路.note: A French Concession street, today's Yan'an Middle Road (eastern stretch).

复兴岛.note: An island in the Huangpu where Chiang Kai-shek stayed and received callers on the eve of the fall of Shanghai.

亨利路.note: French Concession road (Route Paul Henry), today's Xinle Road.

辣斐德路.note: French Concession road (Route Lafayette), today's Fuxing Middle Road.

敏体尼荫路.note: French Concession road, today's South Xizang Road. Book form 'Rue Montauban' matches ch08; historically this was Route Montigny (敏体尼 = Montigny) -- FLAG FOR B10 reconciliation.

丽都花园.note: A Shanghai entertainment garden/ballroom Du frequented.

华懋饭店.note: Sassoon's Cathay Hotel on the Bund (今 Peace Hotel north building).

城隍庙.note: The City God Temple in the old Shanghai city.

金利源码头.note: The China Merchants' Jinliyuan wharf, haunt of young Du's gambling.

郑家木桥.note: A quarter and old bridge on the French Concession edge; book form 'Zhengjia Wooden Bridge', per ch08.

八仙桥.note: A district of the French Concession (lit. 'Eight Immortals Bridge'). Book form 'Baxianqiao', consistent across ch08/13/14/16.

小东门.note: The Small East Gate quarter of the old Shanghai city (per ch08).

共舞台.note: A Shanghai opera theater where Yao Yulan and Yuying performed.

长生桥.note: A place in the old walled city; crop-verified (OCR misread 长生帮).

莫干山.note: The hill resort in Zhejiang where Du kept a villa.

里咸瓜街.note: A street by the money-shop guildhall (then Xiexing Street) in the old city.

金陵东路.note: Today's name for the former Rue du Consulat (法大马路). Book form 'East Jinling Road', per ch08/14/16.

南通.note: The Jiangsu city on the north bank of the Yangtze, Zhang Jian's base.

扬州.note: The Grand Canal city of Subei.

苏北.note: Northern Jiangsu (Subei), the region north of the Yangtze served by the Dada route. Book form "northern Jiangsu", per ch09/12/13/15.

镇江.note: The Yangtze city, Yang Guanbei's home.

天生港.note: The river port near Nantong with Dada's wharf; provisional.

龙潭.note: The 1927 battle where Sun Chuanfang was routed.

海门.note: A county at the Yangtze mouth on the Beisha line.

启东.note: A county at the Yangtze mouth on the Beisha line.

河南路.note: The Shanghai road with the Tianhou Temple.

天后宫.note: The Empress-of-Heaven (Mazu) temple on Henan Road, the boycott body's office.

告罗士打酒店.note: 告罗士打酒店; the Gloucester Hotel, a landmark Hong Kong hotel.

柯士甸道.note: 柯士甸道; Austin Road, Kowloon.

霞飞路.note: 霞飞路; the principal street of the French Concession (Avenue Joffre), today's Huaihai Middle Road.

打铜街.note: 打铜街; a street in central Chongqing, site of the Bank of Communications.

汪山.note: 汪山; a hill district on the south bank of the Yangtze at Chongqing, a wartime villa area.

淳安.note: 淳安; a county in western Zhejiang.

商丘.note: 商丘; a city in eastern Henan.

界首.note: 界首; a town on the Henan–Anhui border, a wartime trans-shipment point between Nationalist and occupied territory.

国际饭店.note: 国际饭店; the Park Hotel on Nanjing Road, then Shanghai's tallest building.

茂名公寓.note: 茂名公寓; the apartment block where Du lived after 1946 (mentioned in a source footnote).

帮会.note: 帮会; the secret-society brotherhoods (青帮 and 洪门) collectively — the book's subject. Rendered ‘the gangs’ or ‘the secret-society gangs’ as context needs; the title's 帮会 is ‘Gangs.’

通草.note: The gang’s internal secret handbooks (通草, also written 通潦, 通钮, or 统抄), recording the patriarchs, the boat system, gang rules, ritual, and argot; kept provisional as no standard English form is attested.

香堂.note: The xiangtang, the altar-hall where initiations and gang rites were held, before the spirit-tablets of the patriarchs.

青皮.note: Literally ‘green skin’; a term for a bold local tough, one proposed origin of the name ‘Green Gang.’

海底.note: The Hongmen's book of rules and ritual.

黄炳权.note: Narrator of this chapter; an electric-power operator in Nanhui and Chuansha who was also warehouse director of the Shanghai Flour Exchange. Romanization provisional.

朱如山.note: A powerful outside speculator in the 1936 flour corner; romanization provisional.

诸广成.note: A standing director of the Flour Exchange; surname 诸 (Zhu), distinct from 朱如山 (also Zhu). Romanization provisional.

卞筱卿.note: Manager of the Nanjing Datong Flour Mill and a co-organizer of the interior mills' association; elected a supervisor of the exchange. Romanization provisional.

荣宗敬.note: 1873–1938; with his brother Rong Desheng, builder of Republican China's largest private industrial group (the Maoxin and Fuxin flour mills and Shenxin cotton mills). Known as the 'Flour King.'

王禹卿.note: Partner and general manager of the Rong family's Maoxin and Fuxin flour mills; a director of the Shanghai Flour Exchange.

王一亭.note: 1867–1938 (born Wang Zhen); comprador, businessman, celebrated Shanghai-School painter and Buddhist-layman philanthropist; longtime chairman of the Flour Exchange.

顾馨一.note: A leader of the exchange's 'gentry faction' alongside Wang Yiting. Romanization provisional.

王叔贤.note: Wang Yiting's second son, who ran up rent debts on an exchange warehouse. Romanization provisional.

胡筠庄.note: Elected a director of the exchange on the Du-Yang slate. Romanization provisional.

面粉交易所.note: 上海面粉交易所, the Shanghai Flour Exchange; a commodity-futures market trading flour by delivery month. Rendered 'the Flour Exchange' / 'the Shanghai Flour Exchange.'

内地面粉厂同业公会.en: the Association of Interior Flour Mills
内地面粉厂同业公会.note: The trade association of the up-country ('interior') flour mills, as opposed to those of Shanghai and Wuxi; Du Yuesheng was its chairman.

茂新.note: 茂新面粉厂, the Rong family's Wuxi flour mill, whose 'Green Warship' brand set the exchange's standard grade.

福新.note: 福新面粉厂, the Rong family's Shanghai flour mill.

阜丰.note: 阜丰面粉厂, a leading Shanghai flour mill, whose 'Red-and-Blue Cart' brand ranked with the Green Warship standard.

大同面粉厂.note: 南京大同面粉厂, the Nanjing Datong Flour Mill, managed by Bian Xiaoqing.

宁海西路.note: The present-day name (Ninghai West Road) of the street formerly called Rue Wagner (华格臬路), where Du's mansion stood.

南汇.note: A rural county on the coast southeast of Shanghai.

川沙.note: A rural county east of Shanghai, in what is now Pudong.

绿兵船.note: The Maoxin/Fuxin mills' flour brand, taken as the exchange's benchmark grade; other mills' flour was discounted against it.

红蓝车.note: The Fufeng mill's flour brand, ranked alongside the Green Warship standard.

袍哥.note: 袍哥; the ‘Gowned Brothers,’ the dominant secret-society brotherhood of Sichuan, analogous to the Green Gang and Hongmen of the lower Yangtze.

孤岛.note: 孤岛; the ‘Solitary Island’ period (1937–1941), when the foreign concessions of Shanghai remained unoccupied islands amid Japanese-held territory until Pearl Harbor.

黄色工会.note: 黄色工会; ‘yellow’ (government- or employer-controlled) labor unions, as opposed to Communist-led ‘red’ ones.
